title: Set Operations & High-Speed Deduplication
summary: Implement practical algorithms: set union (addAll), intersection (retainAll), difference (removeAll), and high-throughput deduplication.
prerequisites: HashSet: How Hash Buckets Guarantee O(1) Lookups
learningObjectives: Master mathematical set algebra in Java: Union, Intersection, Difference, and Subset
Utilize bulk collection methods: addAll(), retainAll(), removeAll(), containsAll()
Apply defensive copying patterns to prevent unintended collection mutation
Implement high-speed stream deduplication and symmetrical difference algorithms
expectedOutcomes: Fluency in expressing relational database joins and group analytics using Java Set algebra
Mastery of high-performance deduplication pipelines across large datasets

activities.title: Practical Context: Venn Diagram Relational Filtering in Data Pipelines

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Venn Diagram Relational Filtering in Data Pipelines
analogy.story:
Imagine a corporate analytics engine evaluating marketing outreach. The database tracks two groups: List A (users who subscribed to the newsletter) and List B (users who made a purchase this month).

The marketing director needs three specific reports:
1. Total Reach: Every customer who either subscribed OR purchased (Union).
2. Engaged Buyers: Customers who BOTH subscribed AND purchased (Intersection).
3. Inactive Subscribers: Customers who subscribed BUT NEVER purchased (Difference).

Rather than executing slow nested database loops, mathematical Set operations compute all three subsets directly in memory at blazing O(N) speeds.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Java's addAll, retainAll, and removeAll methods directly correspond to Union, Intersection, and Set Difference in mathematical set algebra.

activities.title: Mathematical Set Algebra: Union, Intersection, and Asymmetric Difference

keyTakeaways: Set Union (A U B) is executed using setA.addAll(setB)
Set Intersection (A ∩ B) is executed using setA.retainAll(setB)
Set Difference (A \ B) is executed using setA.removeAll(setB)
Subset verification (A ⊆ B) is executed using setB.containsAll(setA)
Always perform defensive copying before applying mutating bulk operations

activities.title: Role-Based Access Control Privilege Verification
activities.description: Trace an enterprise security module evaluating whether a user possesses all permissions required to execute a secure action.

steps.description: Validate edge cases: if required permissions are empty, access is granted; if user has no rights, access is rejected.
Invoke userPermissions.containsAll(requiredPermissions). This checks every element in requiredPermissions against userPermissions in O(M) time.
Test with admin and editor roles. Admin contains both WRITE and AUDIT (true). Editor lacks AUDIT (false).

questions.question: Which method computes the intersection of two sets in Java?
questions.explanation: retainAll() retains only the elements in the invoking set that are contained in the specified collection, which is the definition of mathematical intersection.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to call setA.removeAll(setB) directly without creating a defensive copy?
options: Because removeAll() throws an exception if elements are missing
Because removeAll() permanently mutates setA, destroying its original contents
Because removeAll() also deletes elements from setB
Because removeAll() runs in O(N^2) time
questions.explanation: Bulk methods on Collection mutate the receiver in place. If callers still need the original setA contents, modifying it directly causes severe side effects.

questions.question: What does setB.containsAll(setA) return when setA is empty?
options: true, because the empty set is a subset of every set
questions.explanation: In mathematical set theory and the Java contract, the empty set is a subset of all sets (including another empty set), so containsAll returns true.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of setA.retainAll(setB) when setA and setB are HashSets of sizes N and M respectively?
questions.explanation: retainAll iterates through all N elements of setA and checks if each is contained in setB via setB.contains() which takes O(1) time. The total complexity is O(N).

questions.question: How would you compute the Symmetric Difference of two sets in Java?
questions.answer: Symmetric difference represents all elements that belong to either set A or set B, but NOT to both. In Java, it can be computed using set algebra: 1) Union: `Set<T> union = new HashSet<>(setA); union.addAll(setB);`, 2) Intersection: `Set<T> intersection = new HashSet<>(setA); intersection.retainAll(setB);`, 3) Subtract intersection from union: `union.removeAll(intersection); return union;`. Alternatively: `Set<T> diff = new HashSet<>(setA); setB.forEach(e -> { if (!diff.add(e)) diff.remove(e); });`.

questions.question: What is the most memory-efficient way to deduplicate a 50,000,000-element list in Java?
questions.answer: If data fits in memory, instantiating `new HashSet<>(initialCapacity)` with capacity pre-sized to `(int)(count / 0.75f) + 1` prevents costly table resize passes during ingestion. For primitive numbers, specialized primitive libraries (like Eclipse Collections or Trove) or BitSets avoid object boxing overhead (saving ~24 bytes per integer). If data exceeds heap memory, an external merge sort or disk-backed Bloom Filter / partitioned hash buckets should be used.

questions.question: Why does ArrayList.removeAll(HashSet) perform faster than HashSet.removeAll(ArrayList)?
questions.answer: Because removeAll iterates over the calling collection and queries `contains()` on the argument collection. If you call `hashSet.removeAll(arrayList)`, for every element in the hash set it performs `arrayList.contains()`, which is an O(N) linear scan, resulting in O(N * M) overall time! In contrast, `arrayList.removeAll(hashSet)` performs `hashSet.contains()` for each item, which is O(1), running in linear O(N) total time.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Set Intersection
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement findCommonElements(Set<String> setA, Set<String> setB) that returns a new Set containing only elements present in both sets without mutating the inputs.
hints: Create a defensive copy: new HashSet<>(setA).

practiceProblems.title: Compute Set Union
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement mergeSets(Set<Integer> setA, Set<Integer> setB) that returns a new Set containing all unique elements from both sets.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Set Difference (A minus B)
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement findDifference(Set<String> setA, Set<String> setB) that returns a new Set containing elements that belong to setA but NOT setB.

practiceProblems.title: Verify Subset Membership
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement isSubsetOf(Set<String> subsetCandidate, Set<String> supersetCandidate) returning true if every element in subsetCandidate exists in supersetCandidate.
hints: An empty set is a subset of any set.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Symmetric Difference
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement symmetricDifference(Set<Integer> setA, Set<Integer> setB) returning elements that are in setA or setB, but not in both.
hints: Union contains all elements: union = new HashSet<>(setA); union.addAll(setB).
Intersection contains common elements: inter = new HashSet<>(setA); inter.retainAll(setB).
